hints: Look closely at the shape of the curve at P compared to Q. At P the rate is still rising, but at Q it has flattened into a plateau.
Remember what limits facilitated diffusion when the curve flattens. Think about carrier proteins becoming saturated, and that this is still passive movement affected by kinetic energy but not by ATP.
walkthrough:
**Read the shape of the graph**

Think of this like a busy doorway. At P, the line is still going up, so more substance X means a faster rate. At Q, the line is flat, so adding more X makes no difference.

That flat part tells you something else is now limiting the rate.

**Apply the carrier protein idea**

Facilitated diffusion needs channel or carrier proteins, but it is still passive, so no ATP is used.

At Q, all the proteins are occupied, or saturated. The only way to go faster is to make the existing proteins work faster, for example by giving the molecules more kinetic energy.

**Check what would actually increase the rate**

Raising temperature from $15^{\circ}C$ to $20^{\circ}C$ increases kinetic energy and membrane fluidity, so molecules collide with carriers more often and carriers change shape faster.

That is why the rate at the plateau Q can still be lifted by warming, but not by adding more X, more ATP, or measuring for longer.

options.A: Correct. At Q carriers are saturated, but higher temperature increases kinetic energy and protein activity, so the maximum rate rises.
options.B: Facilitated diffusion is passive and down a concentration gradient, so extra ATP will not drive it faster.
options.C: At Q the curve has plateaued because carriers are saturated, so increasing concentration of X will not increase the rate further.
options.D: Rate is amount moved per unit time, so measuring over a longer time does not change the rate at P.
